'''''Laurus nobilis''''' {{IPAc-en|ˈ|l|ɔːr|ə|s|_|ˈ|n|ɒ|b|ɪ|l|ɪ|s}}<ref>{{Cite Merriam-Webster|Laurus}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://davesgarden.com/guides/botanary/go/3922/ |title=Botanary: nobilis |author=<!--Not stated--> |date=<!--Not stated--> |website=Dave's Garden |publisher= |access-date=December 19, 2022 |quote=}}</ref> is an aromatic [[evergreen]] tree or large [[shrub]] with green, [[Glossary of botanical terms#glabrous|glabrous]] (smooth) leaves. It is in the [[flowering plant]] family [[Lauraceae]]. According to  Muer, Jahn, & Sauerbier, the stem can be 1 metre in diameter and the tree can be as high as 20 metres.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Muer |first1=Thomas |title=Flora Cretica: a complete handbook of all flowering plants, lycopods and ferns occurring on the island of Crete and surrounding islets |last2=Jahn |first2=Ralf |last3=Sauerbier |first3=Herbert |date=2024 |publisher=Kleinsteuber Books |isbn=978-3-9818110-5-6 |location=Karlsruhe}}</ref> It is native to the [[Mediterranean region]] and is used as [[bay leaf]] for seasoning in cooking. Its common names include '''bay tree''' (esp. United Kingdom),<ref name="Stace-2010">{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|author-link = Stace, C. A.|year=2010|title=New Flora of the British Isles|edition=Third|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location = Cambridge, U.K.| isbn=978-0-521-70772-5}}</ref>{{rp|84}} '''bay laurel''', '''sweet bay''', '''true laurel''', '''Grecian laurel''',<ref>{{cite book |last1=Brown |first1=Roland W. | author-link=Roland W. Brown | title=Composition of Scientific Words: A manual of methods and a lexicon of materials for the practice of logotechnics |year=1977 |orig-date=1st Pub. 1954 |publisher=Smithsonian Institutional Press | location=Washington, D.C. | isbn=978-0-87474-286-2 | oclc=4495758 |via=Internet Archive |url=https://archive.org/details/compositionofsci00brow |access-date=27 August 2025}}</ref> or simply '''laurel'''. ''Laurus nobilis'' figures prominently in classical [[Greco-Roman]] culture.

Worldwide, many other kinds of plants in diverse families are also called "bay" or "laurel", generally due to similarity of foliage or aroma to ''Laurus nobilis''.

==Description==
[[File:Laurus nobilis g1.jpg|thumb|A laurel shrub]]
[[File:Laurus nobilis 111.JPG|thumb|''Laurus nobilis'' in pot]]
[[File:Δάφνη του Απόλλωνος ανθισμένη.jpg|thumb|''Laurus nobilis'' in bloom]]
[[File:Loureiro, Laurus nobilis - 55007227262.jpg|thumb|''L. nobilis'' in Brazil]]
The laurel is an [[evergreen]] shrub or small [[tree]], variable in size and sometimes reaching {{convert|7|–|18|m|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name="Stace-2010"/> The genus ''Laurus'' includes three accepted species,<ref name=POWO>{{cite web |title=''Laurus'' L. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:328263-2 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew  |work=Plants of the World Online |access-date=11 February 2024 }}</ref> whose diagnostic key characters often overlap.<ref>[[David Mabberley|Mabberley]], The Plant-Book: A Portable Dictionary of the Vascular Plants, Cambridge University Press, 19 Jun 1997</ref>

The bay laurel is [[dioecy|dioecious]] ([[unisexual]]), with male and female [[flower]]s on separate plants.<ref name="Vaughan-2009" /> Each flower is pale yellow-green, about {{convert|1|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} diameter, and they are borne in pairs beside a leaf. The leaves are glabrous, {{convert|6-12|cm|abbr=on|0}} long and {{convert|2-4|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} broad, with an [[entire leaf|entire]] (untoothed) margin. On some leaves the margin undulates.<ref name="Vaughan-2009" /> The [[fruit]] is a small, shiny black drupe-like berry<ref>{{Cite web |title=Laurus nobilis - Plant Finder |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=281677&isprofile=1&basic=Laurus%20nobilis |access-date=2023-08-23 |website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=Flora Europaea |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=1964 |location=Cambridge |pages=Volume 1 page 246}}</ref> about {{convert|1|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long<ref name="Vaughan-2009" /> that contains one seed.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Konstantinidou, E. |author2=Takos, I. |author3=Merou, T. |year=2008|title=Desiccation and storage behavior of bay laurel (''Laurus nobilis'' L.) seeds|journal=European Journal of Forest Research|volume=127|issue=2|pages=125–131|doi=10.1007/s10342-007-0189-z|bibcode=2008EJFR..127..125K |s2cid=28898196 }}</ref><ref name="Stace-2010"/>

==Ecology==
{{Further|Laurel forest}}
''Laurus nobilis'' is a widespread [[Relict (biology)|relict]] <!--Not a typo--> of the [[laurel forest]]s that originally covered much of the [[Mediterranean Basin]] when the climate of the region was more humid. With the drying of the Mediterranean during the [[Pliocene]] era, the laurel forests gradually retreated, and were replaced by the more drought-tolerant [[sclerophyll]] plant communities familiar today. Most of the last remaining laurel forests around the Mediterranean are believed to have disappeared approximately ten thousand years ago, although some remnants still persist in the mountains of southern [[Turkey]], northern [[Syria]], southern [[Spain]], north-central [[Portugal]], northern [[Morocco]], the [[Canary Islands]] and in [[Madeira]].{{Citation needed|date=March 2025}}

==Human uses==

=== History ===
Early evidence of the use of the plant has been found at [[Ashkelon]] in modern Israel, dating to 7th century BC Judea/Assyria.<ref name="Walton-2022">{{Citation |last=Walton |first=Joshua AU - Santini, Lauren M. |chapter=Spices, Herbs, and Sweeteners |date=2022 |title=T&T Clark Handbook of Food in the Hebrew Bible and Ancient Palestine |pages=163–164 |editor-last=Fu |editor-first=Janling |chapter-url=https://www.bloomsburyfoodlibrary.com/encyclopedia-chapter?docid=b-9780567679826&tocid=b-9780567679826-chapter9 |access-date=2025-07-28 |series=T&T Clark Handbooks |edition=1 |place=London |publisher=T&T Clark |language=en |isbn=978-0-567-67982-6 |editor2-last=Shafer-Elliott |editor2-first=Cynthia |editor3-last=Meyers |editor3-first=Carol}}</ref>

===Food===
The plant is the source of several popular [[herbs]] and one [[spice]] used in a wide variety of recipes, particularly among Mediterranean cuisines.<ref name="Vaughan-2009">{{Cite book |title=The New Oxford Book of Food Plants |last=Vaughan |first=John Griffith |author2=Geissler, Catherine  |author-link=John Griffith Vaughan |year=2009 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford |isbn=978-0-19-954946-7 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UdKxFcen8zgC&q=bay%20laurel&pg=PA150 |access-date=2010-12-31 | page = 150}}</ref> They are typically removed from dishes before serving, although they may also be used as a simple [[Garnish (food)|garnish]]. Whole bay leaves have a long [[shelf life]] of about one year, under normal temperature and humidity. Whole bay leaves are used almost exclusively as flavor agents during the food preparation stage. Ground bay leaves, however, can be ingested safely and are often used in [[soup]]s and [[Stock (food)|stocks]], as well as being a common addition to a [[Bloody Mary (cocktail)|Bloody Mary]]. Dried laurel berries and pressed leaf oil can both be used as robust spices, and the wood can be burnt for strong [[smoking (food)|smoke flavoring]].<ref name="Green-2006">{{Cite book |title=Field Guide to Herbs & Spices |last=Green |first=Aliza |year=2006 |publisher=Quirk Books |location=Philadelphia |isbn=978-1-59474-082-4 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oGaF5FZ-sMMC&q=bay%20laurel%20berries&pg=PA17 |access-date=2010-12-31 }}</ref>

===Ornamental===
''Laurus nobilis'' is widely cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] in regions with [[Mediterranean climate|Mediterranean]] or [[oceanic climate]]s, and as a house plant or greenhouse plant in colder regions. It is used in [[topiary]] to create single erect stems with ball-shaped, box-shaped or twisted crowns; also for low hedges. However, it is slow-growing and may take several years to reach the desired height.<ref name="Brickell-2008">{{cite book | editor-last = Brickell | editor-first = Christopher | title = The Royal Horticultural Society A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants | year = 2008 | page = 614 | publisher = Dorling Kindersley | location = United Kingdom | isbn = 978-1-4053-3296-5}}</ref> Together with a gold form, ''L. nobilis'' 'Aurea'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/99463/Laurus-nobilis-Aurea/Details |title=Laurus nobilis 'Aurea' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 1 October 2020}}</ref> and a willow-leaved form ''L. nobilis'' f. ''angustifolia'',<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/74790/i-Laurus-nobilis-i-f-i-angustifolia-i/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder – ''Laurus nobilis'' f. ''angustifolia'' | access-date = 19 March 2018}}</ref> it has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name="RHS">{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/9876/Laurus-nobilis/Details | title = ''Laurus nobilis'' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 1 October 2020}}</ref>

One of the most important pests affecting ornamental laurels is caused by the [[Triozidae|jumping plant louse]] ''[[Trioza alacris]]'', which induces the curling and thickening of the edge of the leaves for the development of the insect's [[Nymph (biology)|nymphs]], eventually creating a necrosed [[gall]].<ref name="De Alfonso-2014">{{Cite book|chapter-url=http://www.sech.info/ACTAS/Acta%20n%C2%BA%2068.%20VI%20Jornadas%20Ib%C3%A9ricas%20de%20Horticultura%20Ornamental/Sanidad%20Vegetal/Evaluaci%C3%B3n%20de%20diferentes%20m%C3%A9todos%20de%20control%20de%20plagas%20en%20cultivo%20de%20laurel%20ornamental%20e%20impacto%20en%20la%20fauna%20%C3%BAtil%20asociada.pdf|chapter=Evaluación de diferentes métodos de control de plagas en cultivo de laurel ornamental e impacto en la fauna útil asociada|first1=M.|last1=De Alfonso|first2=A.|last2=Olmeda1|first3=E.|last3=Rodrigo|first4=P.|last4=Xamaní|first5=A.|last5=Sánchez–Domingo|first6=R.|last6=Laborda|year=2014|title=VI Jornadas Ibéricas de Horticultura Ornamental: Las buenas prácticas agrícolas en horticultura ornamental|isbn=978-84-617-3020-9|pages=50–51}}</ref> The species is also affected by the [[scale insect]] ''[[Coccus hesperidum]]''.<ref name="De Alfonso-2014" />

===Alternative medicine===
[[Image:LaurusNobilisEssOil.png|thumb|''Laurus nobilis'' essential oil in clear glass vial]]
In [[herbal medicine]], [[Aqueous solution|aqueous]] [[extract]]s of bay laurel have been used as an [[astringent]] and salve for open wounds.<ref name="Nayak-2006">{{Cite journal |pmid=16597335 |year=2006 |last1=Nayak |first1=S |last2=Nalabothu |first2=P |last3=Sandiford |first3=S |last4=Bhogadi |first4=V |last5=Adogwa |first5=A |title=Evaluation of wound healing activity of Allamanda cathartica. L. and Laurus nobilis. L. extracts on rats |volume=6 |article-number=12 |doi=10.1186/1472-6882-6-12 |pmc=1456996 |journal=BMC Complementary and Alternative Medicine |doi-access=free }}.</ref> It is also used in [[massage therapy]] and [[aromatherapy]].<ref name="Encyclopedia of Herbs">{{cite web |url=http://www.allnatural.net/herbpages/bay-laurel.shtml |title=Bay Laurel: Laurus nobilis |author=Encyclopedia of Herbs |publisher=AllNatural.net |access-date=2010-12-31 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20101119205731/http://allnatural.net/herbpages/bay-laurel.shtml| archive-date= 19 November 2010 | url-status= live}}</ref> A [[folk medicine|folk remedy]] for rashes caused by [[poison ivy]], [[poison oak]], and [[Urtica dioica|stinging nettle]] is a [[poultice]] soaked in boiled bay leaves.<ref>{{Cite book |title=The Faerie's Guide to Green Magick from the Garden |last=Wood |first=Jamie |author2=Steinke, Lisa  |year=2010 |publisher=Random House |location=New York |isbn=978-1-58761-354-8 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=61Vm30HszfkC&q=bay%20laurel&pg=PA43 |access-date=2010-12-31 | page = 43}}</ref> The Roman naturalist [[Pliny the Elder]] listed a variety of conditions which laurel oil was supposed to treat: paralysis, spasms, [[sciatica]], bruises, headaches, [[catarrh]]s, ear infections, and rheumatism.<ref>{{cite book| title=Natural History| author=Pliny the Elder| page=XXIII.43}}</ref>

==Symbolism==
===Greece===
In [[Greek language|Greek]], the plant is called {{lang|el|δάφνη}} {{lang|el-Latn|dáphnē}}, after the mythic mountain nymph [[Daphne|of the same name]]. In the myth of [[Apollo and Daphne]], the god [[Apollo]] fell in love with Daphne, a priestess of [[Gaia]] (Mother Earth), and when he tried to seduce her she pleaded for help to Gaia, who transported her to [[Crete]]. In Daphne's place Gaia left a laurel tree, from which Apollo fashioned [[Laurel wreath|wreaths]] to console himself.<ref>{{cite book| title=The Greek Myths: Part 1| first=Robert |last=Graves| publisher=Penguin Books| year=1955 |pages=21.K–21.L}}</ref>

Other versions of the myth, including that of the Roman poet [[Ovid]], state that Daphne was transformed directly into a laurel tree.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.tkline.freeserve.co.uk/Metamorph.htm%23_Toc64105470 |title=The Metamorphoses |access-date=2017-11-17 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://archive.today/20050419213646/http://www.tkline.freeserve.co.uk/Metamorph.htm%23_Toc64105470 |archive-date=April 19, 2005 |translator-first=A. S. |translator-last=Kline |year=2000}}</ref>

Bay laurel was used to fashion the [[laurel wreath]] of [[ancient Greece]], a symbol of highest status. A wreath of bay laurels was given as the prize at the [[Pythian Games]] because the games were in honor of Apollo, and the laurel was one of his symbols. According to the poet [[Lucian]], the priestess of Apollo known as the [[Pythia]] reputedly chewed laurel leaves from a sacred tree growing inside the temple to induce the {{lang|grc-Latn|enthusiasmos}} (trance) from which she uttered the oracular prophecies for which she was famous.<ref>{{cite book|title=Delphi|last=Scott |first=Michael|publisher=Princeton University Press|year=2014|page=20}}</ref> Some accounts starting in the fourth century BC describe her as shaking a [[Laurel wreath|laurel branch]] while delivering her prophecies. Those who received promising omens from the Pythia were crowned with laurel wreaths as a symbol of Apollo's favor.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Lore of Spices |first=J. O. |last=Swahn |publisher=Random House |year=1991 |page=40}}</ref>

===Rome===
[[File:Francesco_Petrarca00.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Petrarch]], laurated poet, father of [[Renaissance humanism|humanism]]]]
The symbolism carried over to [[Roman culture]], which held the laurel as a symbol of victory.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Compendium of symbolic and ritual plants in Europe |volume=1 |last1=De Cleene |first1=Marcel |last2=Lejeune |first2=Marie Claire |year=2003 |publisher=Man & Culture |oclc=482791069 |page=129}}</ref> It was also associated with immortality,<ref>{{cite book| url=https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.02.0137%3Abook%3D15%3Achapter%3D39| title=Natural History Book XV.39| author=Pliny the Elder}}</ref> with ritual purification, prosperity and health.<ref name="Giesecke-2014">{{cite book| title=The Mythology of Plants: Botanical Lore from Ancient Greece and Rome| first=Annette |last=Giesecke| publisher=J. Paul Getty Museum| year=2014| pages=35–36}}</ref><ref name="Pliny the Elder">{{cite book| title=Natural History |at=Book XV, 35| author=Pliny the Elder}}</ref> It is also the source of the words ''[[bachelor's degree|baccalaureate]]'' and ''[[poet laureate]]'', as well as the expressions "assume the laurel" and "resting on one's laurels".{{Citation needed|date=March 2025}}

[[Pliny the Elder]] stated that the laurel was not permitted for "profane" uses – lighting it on fire at altars "for the propitiation of divinities" was strictly forbidden, because "it is very evident that the laurel protests against such usage by crackling as it does in the fire, thus, in a manner, giving expression to its abhorrence of such treatment".<ref>{{cite book| url=https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.02.0137%3Abook%3D15%3Achapter%3D40| title=Natural History |at=Book XV.135| author=Pliny the Elder}}</ref>

Laurel was closely associated with the Roman Emperors, beginning with [[Augustus]]. Two Laurel trees flanked the entrance to Augustus' house on the [[Palatine Hill]] in Rome, which itself was connected to the [[Temple of Apollo Palatinus]], which Augustus had built. Thus, the laurels had the dual purpose of advertising Augustus' victory in the Civil Wars and his close association with Apollo.<ref name="Giesecke-2014"/> [[Suetonius]] relates the story of Augustus' wife, and Rome's first Empress, [[Livia]], who planted a sprig of laurel on the grounds of her [[Villa of Livia|villa]] at [[Prima Porta]] after an eagle dropped a hen with the sprig clutched in its beak onto her lap.<ref name="Suetonius">{{cite book| title=Galba |at=Book 7, 1| author=Suetonius}}</ref> The sprig grew into a full-size tree which fostered an entire grove of laurel trees, which were in turn added to by subsequent Emperors when they celebrated a [[Roman triumph|triumph]]. The emperors in the [[Julio-Claudian]] dynasty all sourced their [[Laurel wreath]]s from the original tree planted by Livia. It was taken as an omen of the impending end of the Julio-Claudian dynasty that in the reign of [[Nero]] the entire grove died, shortly before he was assassinated.<ref name="Suetonius"/> Rome's second Emperor [[Tiberius]] wore wreaths of laurel whenever there was stormy weather because it was widely believed that Laurel trees were immune to lightning strikes, affording protection to those who brandished it.<ref name="McCartney-1929">{{cite journal| title=Why Did Tiberius Wear Laurel in the Form of a Crown During Thunder Storms| first=Eugene S. |last=McCartney| journal=Classical Philology| year=1929| volume=24| issue=2| pages=201–203| doi=10.1086/361124| s2cid=162098134}}</ref><ref>{{cite book| title=Tiberius, 69| author=Suetonius}}</ref><ref name="Pliny the Elder"/> One reason for this belief is because laurel crackles loudly when on fire. It led ancient Romans to believe the plant was inhabited by a "heavenly fire [[Daemon (classical mythology)|demon]]", and was therefore "immune" from outer threats like fire or lightning.<ref name="McCartney-1929"/>

In modern Italy, laurel wreaths are worn as a crown by graduating school students.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Laurea: perché si incorona il laureato con l'alloro? {{!}} Giftsitter |trans-title=Graduation: Why do you crown the graduate with the laurel? |url=https://giftsitter.com/it/blog/laurea-perche-si-incorona-il-laureato-con-lalloro |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180414010850/https://giftsitter.com/it/blog/laurea-perche-si-incorona-il-laureato-con-lalloro |archive-date=2018-04-14 |access-date=2025-09-11 |website=Giftsitter |language=it-IT |author=Gabriella Massara}}</ref>{{better source needed|date=September 2025}}

===East Asia===
An early Chinese [[etiological myth]] for the [[phases of the moon]] involved a great forest or tree which quickly grew and lost its leaves and flowers every month. After the [[Sui dynasty|Sui]] and [[Tang dynasty|Tang]] [[list of Chinese dynasties|dynasties]], this was sometimes connected to a woodsman named [[Wu Gang]], sentenced to cut at a self-repairing tree as a punishment for varying offenses. The tree was originally identified as a {{lang|zh|{{linktext|桂}}}} (''guì'') and described in the terms of the [[sweet osmanthus|osmanthus]]<!--sources at Wu Gang--> (''Osmanthus fragrans'', now known in Chinese as the {{lang|zh|{{linktext|桂花}}}} or "''gui'' flower"), whose blossoms are still used to flavor [[osmanthus wine|wine]] and confections for the [[Mid-Autumn Festival]]. However, in English, it is often associated with the more well-known [[Chinese cassia|cassia]] (''Cinnamomum cassia'', now known in Chinese as the {{lang|zh|{{linktext|肉桂}}}} or "meat ''gui''") while, in modern Chinese, it has instead become associated with the Mediterranean laurel. By the [[Qing dynasty]], the ''[[chengyu]]'' "pluck osmanthus in the [[moon toad|Toad]] Palace" ({{lang|zh|{{linktext|蟾宫折桂}}}}, ''Chángōng zhé guì'') meant passing the [[keju|imperial examination]]s,<ref name="Brendon-1927">Brendon, Juliet et al. ''The Moon Year: A Record of Chinese Customs and Festivals'', [https://books.google.com/books?id=3vUZMgM5bhQC&pg=PA410 p. 410]. Kelly & Walsh, 1927. Reprinted Routledge (Abingdon), 2011. Accessed 13 November 2013.</ref><ref>Zdic (2013). {{lang|zh|[http://www.zdic.net/c/e/a7/196726.htm "蟾宫折桂"]}}. Accessed 13 November 2013. {{in lang|zh}}</ref><ref>{{lang|zh|杜近芳}} [Du Jinfang] (2003). [http://tieba.baidu.com/p/84960300?pn=2 {{lang|zh|《红楼梦汉英习语词典》}}] ["A Dictionary of Chinese Idioms in the ''[[Dream of the Red Chamber]]''"]. Accessed 13 November 2013. {{in lang|en|zh}}</ref> which were held around the time of the lunar festival. The similar association in Europe of laurels with victory and success led to its translation into Chinese as the {{lang|zh|{{linktext|月桂}}}} or "Moon ''gui''".{{Citation needed|date=March 2025}}

===Finland===
[[File:Kaskinen.vaakuna.svg|thumb|upright=0.6|The laurel leaves in the right side of the coat of arms of [[Kaskinen]]]]
The laurel leaves in the coat of arms of [[Kaskinen]], [[Finland]] ({{langx|sv|Kaskö}}), may have been meant to refer to local flowering, but its origin may also be in the name of the family Bladh ({{langx|sv|blad}}; 'leaf'); two members of the family – a father and a son – acquired both [[town rights]] and the status of staple town for the village at the time.<ref>{{cite book| title= Suomen kunnallisvaakunat | publisher= Suomen Kunnallisliitto | year= 1982 | page= 117 | isbn= 951-773-085-3 | language= fi}}</ref><ref>Boyko, Dm. A. (2013). ''Геральдика Великого Княжества Финляндского'' [''Heraldry of the Grand Duchy of Finland'']. Zaporizhzhia. {{in lang|ru}}</ref>

==Chemical constituents==
The most abundant component found in laurel [[essential oil]] is [[1,8-cineole]], also called eucalyptol. The leaves contain about 1.3% essential oils (''ol. lauri folii''), consisting of 45% [[eucalyptol]], 12% other [[terpene]]s, 8–12% [[terpinyl acetate]], 3–4% [[sesquiterpene]]s, 3% [[methyleugenol]], and other α- and β-[[pinene]]s, [[phellandrene]], [[linalool]], [[geraniol]], and [[terpineol]].<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1021/jf0306237| pmid = 15030218| title = Volatile Constituents and Key Odorants in Leaves, Buds, Flowers, and Fruits of ''Laurus'' nobilisL| journal = Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry| volume = 52| issue = 6| pages = 1601–6| year = 2004| last1 = Kilic| first1 = Ayben| last2 = Hafizoglu| first2 = Harzemsah| last3 = Kollmannsberger| first3 = Hubert| last4 = Nitz| first4 = Siegfried| bibcode = 2004JAFC...52.1601K}}</ref> It contains [[lauric acid]] also.{{Citation needed|date=July 2019}}

Both essential and fatty oils are present in the fruit. The fruit is pressed and water-extracted to obtain these products. The fruit contains up to 30% fatty oils and about 1% essential oils (terpenes, sesquiterpenes, [[Alcohol (chemistry)|alcohol]]s, and [[ketone]]s). This laurel oil is the characteristic ingredient of [[Aleppo soap]]. The chemical compound [[lauroside B]] has been isolated from ''Laurus nobilis''.<ref>{{cite journal | pmid = 21188975 | year = 2011 | last1 = Panza | first1 = E | last2 = Tersigni | first2 = M | last3 = Iorizzi | first3 = M | last4 = Zollo | first4 = F | last5 = De Marino | first5 = S | last6 = Festa | first6 = C | last7 = Napolitano | first7 = M | last8 = Castello | first8 = G | last9 = Ialenti | first9 = A | display-authors = 8| title = Lauroside B, a megastigmane glycoside from Laurus nobilis (bay laurel) leaves, induces apoptosis in human melanoma cell lines by inhibiting NF-κB activation | volume = 74 | issue = 2 | pages = 228–33 | doi = 10.1021/np100688g | journal = Journal of Natural Products| bibcode = 2011JNAtP..74..228P }}</ref>
